objectives: Trace paleontology's founders from Smith and Cuvier to Walcott and Andrews.
Summarize the 20th-c synthesis of paleobiology — Simpson, Gould-Eldredge, Raup-Sepkoski.
Survey modern frontiers — molecular paleobiology, paleogenomics, computational tomography.

slides.title: Founders: from strata to bone wars (1800-1920s)
slides.body:
**Paleontology** = the science of ancient life. Sits at the intersection of geology, biology, and chemistry. Its emergence as a discipline required two prior intellectual moves: (1) recognizing that fossils represent extinct organisms (not curiosities, sport of nature, or biblical-flood victims); (2) accepting that the Earth is unimaginably old.

**William Smith** (1769-1839) — English canal-surveyor known as the 'Father of English Geology'. Discovered the **principle of faunal succession** (1815): sedimentary strata contain characteristic fossil assemblages, and the same assemblages appear in the same order wherever the strata are found. Smith's geological map of England + Wales (1815) — the first nationwide geological map — used fossil content to correlate distant outcrops. The principle remains the conceptual backbone of biostratigraphy: every stratigrapher in 2026 still uses Smith's logic when assigning a layer a relative age from its fossils.

**Georges Cuvier** (1769-1832) — French anatomist + permanent secretary of the Académie des Sciences. Founded vertebrate paleontology + comparative anatomy. Demonstrated rigorously, via comparison of fossil bones with living relatives, that fossil mastodons + mosasaurs + pterosaurs represented species no longer alive — **extinction is real**. Cuvier was a catastrophist (sudden upheavals reshape the Earth) + opposed Lamarck's transmutation. His method of inferring whole organisms from fragments — the 'principle of correlation of parts' — set the methodological standard for the field.

**Richard Owen** (1804-1892) — British comparative anatomist + founder of the Natural History Museum (London, 1881). In 1842 Owen coined **Dinosauria** ('terrible lizards') to unite *Megalosaurus*, *Iguanodon*, + *Hylaeosaurus* as a distinct clade of giant terrestrial reptiles. Owen was Darwin's intellectual rival but contributed enormously — descriptions of *Archaeopteryx* (1863), terror birds, and many extinct vertebrates.

**The Bone Wars (1870s-1890s)**: bitter feud between **Edward Drinker Cope** (Philadelphia) + **Othniel Charles Marsh** (Yale) in the American West. Funded by railroads + the U.S. Geological Survey; competed to describe new dinosaurs. Together they named >130 dinosaur species — *Triceratops*, *Stegosaurus*, *Allosaurus*, *Diplodocus*, *Brontosaurus* (Marsh, later synonymized with *Apatosaurus*, re-validated 2015). The feud became personal — sabotaged digs, dynamited bones, scientific name-flooding — but launched American paleontology.

**Charles H. Sternberg** (1850-1943) + his sons George, Charles M., + Levi — the most prolific North American fossil hunters of the era; mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, ceratopsians, hadrosaurs across Kansas, Wyoming, Montana. The Sternberg dynasty's specimens fill museum halls from Ottawa to New York to Berlin.

**Charles Doolittle Walcott** (1850-1927) — Smithsonian Secretary. **Burgess Shale** discovery (British Columbia, 1909): exquisitely preserved Cambrian soft-bodied fauna — *Anomalocaris*, *Opabinia*, *Wiwaxia*, *Hallucigenia*, *Marrella* — the first window into the **Cambrian Explosion**. Walcott collected 65000+ specimens. Their reinterpretation by Whittington + Conway Morris + Briggs (1970s) reshaped views of early animal evolution.

**Roy Chapman Andrews** (1884-1960) — American explorer + Director of the AMNH. Led the **Central Asiatic Expeditions** to Mongolia (1922-1930) — discovered Velociraptor, Protoceratops, Oviraptor + the first identified **dinosaur nests** + eggs at the Flaming Cliffs of Bayanzag. Allegedly the model for Indiana Jones. Established the Gobi Desert as a premier Mesozoic fossil locality.

By 1930, paleontology had its empirical foundation: thousands of described species, stratigraphic correlation worldwide, and the realization that life's history is far stranger + more discontinuous than any pre-Darwinian imagination.

slides.title: The 20th-c synthesis: paleobiology becomes evolutionary biology
slides.body:
Through the early 20th c, paleontology was largely descriptive — naming specimens, building stratigraphic columns. The mid-century **paleobiology revolution** made it a quantitative + evolutionary science.

**George Gaylord Simpson** (1902-1984) — American paleontologist at the AMNH + Columbia. *Tempo and Mode in Evolution* (1944) — fused paleontology with the Modern Synthesis of population genetics + selection (Fisher, Wright, Haldane, Dobzhansky, Mayr). Argued the fossil record was *compatible* with microevolutionary mechanisms scaled up. Introduced **quantum evolution**: rapid transitions between adaptive zones. *The Major Features of Evolution* (1953). Simpson legitimated paleontology as a partner in evolutionary theory — not a separate descriptive science.

**Punctuated equilibrium** — **Niles Eldredge** + **Stephen Jay Gould** (1972, in *Models in Paleobiology*): the fossil record shows long periods of morphological stasis interrupted by relatively rapid (geologically) speciation events. Stasis is *real* — not a sampling artifact. Speciation typically occurs in small peripheral populations (consistent with Mayr's peripatric speciation) + then those species spread + dominate the record. Contrasted with the prior textbook view of **phyletic gradualism**. Now widely accepted as describing many (not all) lineages — clams, foraminifera, bryozoans show clear punctuation; mammals + some others show more gradual change. Gould's *The Structure of Evolutionary Theory* (2002) is the canonical treatment.

**David Raup** (1933-2015) + **Jack Sepkoski** (1948-1999) — American paleobiologists, U Chicago. Sepkoski's compendium of marine genera (1982, 1992) — a decade-long database of >36000 marine genera through Phanerozoic time — enabled the first quantitative analysis of biodiversity through deep time. Raup + Sepkoski (1982) **Big Five mass extinctions**: Ordovician-Silurian, Late Devonian, Permian-Triassic, Triassic-Jurassic, K-Pg. Their statistical work established that mass extinctions are distinct events, not noise. Raup's *Extinction: Bad Genes or Bad Luck?* (1991). Sepkoski's three evolutionary faunas: Cambrian (trilobite-dominated) → Paleozoic (brachiopod-crinoid) → Modern (mollusk-gastropod-vertebrate).

**Cambrian re-revolution** — **Harry Whittington** (1916-2010), Cambridge; + his students **Simon Conway Morris** + **Derek Briggs** — re-described Walcott's Burgess Shale fauna (1971-1985). Discovered Walcott's specimens were not all primitive crustaceans but a wildly diverse + bizarre assemblage of body plans, many representing extinct phyla or stem-group bilaterians. Gould popularized this in *Wonderful Life* (1989) arguing the Cambrian was a 'disparity' explosion + history was contingent. Conway Morris pushed back (*The Crucible of Creation*, 1998) — many Burgess Shale animals were not 'weird' but stem-group representatives of living phyla; **convergence** would have produced similar forms even if the tape were re-run. The debate still defines macroevolutionary thinking.

**Other 20th-c giants**: **Alfred Romer** (vertebrate paleontology textbook 1933, the standard for decades); **Edwin Colbert** (dinosaur paleontology); **Robert Bakker** + **John Ostrom** (hot-blooded dinosaurs hypothesis 1970s); **Jack Horner** (dinosaur parental care, growth); **Mary Schweitzer** (soft tissue + biomolecules; see next slide).

By 2000, paleontology was a quantitative discipline using statistics, geochemistry, biomechanics, + phylogenetics — and a full partner in evolutionary biology.

slides.title: Modern paleontology: molecules, genomes, and CT scans
slides.body:
The 21st c has transformed paleontology into a molecular + computational science. Several frontiers:

**Molecular paleobiology** — extracting + interpreting biomolecules from ancient specimens.
- **Ancient DNA (aDNA)** — pioneered by **Svante Pääbo** (Max Planck Leipzig; Physiology or Medicine Nobel 2022). Pääbo's lab sequenced the first Neanderthal mtDNA (1997), the Neanderthal nuclear genome (2010), and **discovered the Denisovans** from a finger bone fragment in 2010 — a previously unknown hominin lineage identified solely from its DNA. aDNA from horses (Orlando 2013, 700-kya horse genome), bears, mammoths, + many Pleistocene megafauna is now routine; DNA degrades exponentially with time so genomes >1 Mya are at the edge of feasibility (Kjær 2022 environmental DNA from 2-Myr Greenland sediments).
- **Paleoproteomics** — ancient proteins survive far longer than DNA because peptides bind tightly to mineral surfaces. **John Asara** (Beth Israel Deaconess + Harvard) + **Mary Schweitzer** (NC State): 2007 mass-spec recovery of collagen peptides from a **68-Mya T. rex** femur (Schweitzer et al. 2005, 2007). The finding was controversial (contamination debates) but confirmed by independent labs + extended to hadrosaurs + other Mesozoic specimens. **Enrico Cappellini** (Copenhagen) pushed paleoproteomics into the deep past — enamel proteomes of 1.77-Myr Dmanisi hominins + 1.9-Myr rhinos.
- **Soft-tissue preservation** — **Mary Schweitzer**'s 2005 *Science* paper reported flexible, transparent, branching structures resembling blood vessels in a *T. rex* (MOR 1125). Skeptics proposed bacterial biofilms; Schweitzer's group + **Alida Bailleul** + the Beijing IVPP have continued to characterize these structures with antibody staining, mass spec, + microscopy. Bailleul (2020) reported cell + nuclear preservation in a 75-Mya *Hypacrosaurus* via histological + histochemical evidence.

**Paleogenomics + phylogenomics** — genome-scale data resolves long-standing questions: bird-crocodile sister relationship, placental mammal radiation timing, the position of turtles. Hybrid genomes (Neanderthal + Denisovan in modern humans, 1-4%) are uncovered routinely.

**Computational tomography (CT) + 3D imaging** — non-destructive examination of fossils in matrix or skull braincases. Synchrotron + micro-CT reveals teeth still in their crypts, inner-ear canals (used to infer hearing range + posture), brain endocasts. Lawrence Witmer, Larry Witmer's lab, Stephanie Pierce + Catherine Forster routinely publish CT-based reconstructions. 3D printing lets paleontologists physically test biomechanical models.

**Geochemical proxies** — stable isotopes (δ¹⁸O for temperature, δ¹³C for diet, ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr for provenance), trace elements, biomarker lipids let paleontologists reconstruct ancient temperatures, atmospheric CO₂, diets, migrations, even seasonality of individual lives.

**Big-data paleobiology** — the **Paleobiology Database (PBDB)** (founded by **John Alroy** 1998+) aggregates >1.5M fossil occurrences globally + drives sampling-standardized diversity curves, biogeographic analyses, + meta-studies. Open data has changed the field.

**Machine learning** — automated fossil identification (Hsiang + Pearson 2019 foraminifera CNN), morphometric analysis, phylogenetic inference, + image segmentation are now standard tools.

Modern paleontology synthesizes the descriptive heritage of Smith + Cuvier with the statistical apparatus of Raup + Sepkoski + the molecular tools of Pääbo + Schweitzer. The discipline has never been more interdisciplinary, and the next century promises to test biological questions — origins of major clades, mechanisms of macroevolution, biotic responses to climate change — at unprecedented resolution.

**Next**: deep time + the geologic time scale + how paleontologists actually date the strata.

question.question: Reason from Smith's principle of faunal succession to relative dating
question.goal: Given two outcrops 200 km apart with overlapping fossil assemblages, derive the relative age relationship.

steps.prompt: Outcrop A (bottom-up): layers a1, a2, a3 contain trilobites of type T1; brachiopods of type B1; trilobites of type T2. Outcrop B (bottom-up): layers b1, b2, b3 contain brachiopods of type B1; trilobites of type T2; ammonites of type A1. What does faunal succession tell us about A2 vs B1?

acceptedAnswers: A2 and B1 contain the same fossil B1 so are same age

steps.reveal: Smith's principle: where strata contain the same fossil assemblage, they are the same relative age. Layer A2 (B1) + layer B1 (B1) share brachiopod B1 + thus are correlative — even though they are 200 km apart + lithologically may differ.

acceptedAnswers: Both contain T2 so are same age

steps.reveal: Both A3 + B2 contain trilobite T2 = correlative. Now we have two tie points (A2-B1 + A3-B2), giving the relative age order: A1 < A2 = B1 < A3 = B2 < B3.

steps.prompt: B3 contains ammonite A1, which appears nowhere in outcrop A. What can we conclude about the post-A3 history at the A site?

acceptedAnswers: A's record ends or contains an unconformity younger than A3
A is missing the A1 interval

steps.reveal: B3 (with A1 ammonite) is younger than A3 (with T2). Outcrop A's record stops at A3 — either erosion removed the equivalent of B3 from site A, or deposition never occurred (unconformity / hiatus). Faunal succession lets us not only correlate but identify gaps in the record.

steps.prompt: What characteristic must T2 + B1 + A1 share to function as **index fossils**?

acceptedAnswers: wide geographic distribution + short stratigraphic range + abundant + easily recognized

hints: What makes a fossil useful for global correlation?
steps.reveal: Index fossils must be: (1) **wide geographic distribution** (so they show up in many outcrops), (2) **short stratigraphic range** (a narrow time window — otherwise correlation is imprecise), (3) **abundant** (so they're actually found), + (4) **morphologically distinctive + easily identified**. Trilobites + ammonites + conodonts + foraminifera + graptolites all satisfy these criteria + are the workhorses of Phanerozoic biostratigraphy.

question.question: Why is Walcott's Burgess Shale (1909) — and its later re-description by Whittington + Conway Morris + Briggs — so foundational to paleobiology?
options: It contains the oldest known dinosaurs.

The Burgess Shale (Cambrian, ~508 Mya) is a **soft-bodied Lagerstätte** preserving non-mineralized organisms — *Anomalocaris*, *Opabinia*, *Wiwaxia*, *Marrella*, *Hallucigenia* + many others — that are almost never preserved elsewhere. Walcott collected 65000+ specimens (1909-1924). Whittington + students Conway Morris + Briggs re-described them (1971-1985), demonstrating that the Cambrian fauna was vastly more morphologically diverse ('disparate') than the modern fauna + included stem-group representatives of many living phyla + some extinct lineages with no clear modern affinity. The site is foundational because: (1) it provides our clearest window into the **Cambrian Explosion** + the origins of complex animal life; (2) it forces paleontologists to confront preservation bias (most ancient organisms left no record); (3) it generated the disparity-vs-convergence debate (Gould 1989 vs Conway Morris 1998) central to macroevolutionary theory; (4) it has been joined by similar Cambrian Lagerstätten — Chengjiang (Yunnan, China, 518 Mya) + Sirius Passet (Greenland) + Emu Bay (Australia) — to give a global view of early animal evolution.
It is the oldest fossil site on Earth.
question.explanation: Burgess Shale (Walcott 1909) is a Cambrian (~508 Mya) Lagerstätte preserving soft-bodied organisms; re-described by Whittington + Conway Morris + Briggs (1971-1985); revealed Cambrian disparity + stem-group phyla; foundational for understanding the Cambrian Explosion + the disparity-vs-convergence debate (Gould 1989 vs Conway Morris 1998); joined by Chengjiang + Sirius Passet + Emu Bay.

hints: What kind of preservation does it show?
What macroevolutionary debate did it spawn?
slides.workedSolution: Burgess Shale (Walcott 1909) is a Cambrian Lagerstätte preserving soft-bodied fauna — *Anomalocaris*, *Opabinia*, *Marrella*, *Hallucigenia*. Re-described 1971-1985 by Whittington + students. Forced reckoning with preservation bias + Cambrian disparity. Spawned Gould vs Conway Morris contingency-vs-convergence debate. Joined by Chengjiang + Sirius Passet + Emu Bay.

question.question: Designing a 21st-c paleontology dig
question.prompt: You lead a paleontology team funded to explore a previously unstudied Late Cretaceous (~70 Mya) terrestrial outcrop in central Mongolia. You have a 3-yr budget for fieldwork, a small team of geologists + paleontologists + geochemists, + access to a CT facility, an aDNA + paleoproteomics lab (collaborators in Copenhagen), + the Paleobiology Database. Sketch your research plan. Address: (1) what initial reconnaissance + stratigraphy you would do to date the strata + correlate them with known Mongolian Late Cretaceous formations (Djadochta, Nemegt — Andrews's 1920s work + descendants); (2) what excavation + curation strategy would maximize both descriptive yield (named taxa) + downstream molecular work (e.g., what to keep frozen, what conditions preserve collagen + cells); (3) how you would deploy CT scanning + 3D imaging to extract data from articulated specimens still in matrix; (4) how you would design the geochemistry program (δ¹⁸O for paleotemperature, δ¹³C for diet) for a multi-isotope reconstruction of the paleoenvironment; (5) what role open data + PBDB submissions play in maximizing scientific impact; (6) what 21st-c question (e.g., trans-Pacific dispersal, K-Pg precursor signals, theropod soft-tissue, dinosaur growth) you would frame the dig around. Explain how this plan synthesizes the descriptive heritage of Smith + Cuvier + Walcott + Andrews with the molecular + computational frontiers of Pääbo + Schweitzer + Witmer + Alroy.

question.question: Cope + Marsh's Bone Wars (c. 1870-1899) produced ~130 named dinosaur species. Of those, recent (2020) revisions estimate ~50% are still considered valid (the rest are junior synonyms or *nomina dubia*). How many valid dinosaur species, to the nearest whole number, did Cope + Marsh contribute?
question.hint: $130 \times 0.50 = 65$. Even after a century of synonymization + revision, the Bone Wars gave us a substantial fraction of all named Mesozoic dinosaurs — *Triceratops*, *Stegosaurus*, *Allosaurus*, *Diplodocus*, *Apatosaurus*, *Camarasaurus* — + remains the most productive episode in North American vertebrate paleontology.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, narrate paleontology's arc from William Smith's 1815 stratigraphic map through Simpson's 1944 *Tempo and Mode* to Pääbo's 2022 Nobel + Schweitzer's soft-tissue work.
question.rubric: Mentions: William Smith's 1815 principle of faunal succession + Cuvier's establishment of extinction + comparative anatomy founded the descriptive science. Owen 1842 coined Dinosauria. The Cope-Marsh Bone Wars (1870s-1890s) + Sternberg + Walcott's 1909 Burgess Shale + Andrews's 1920s Mongolian expeditions built the empirical base. Simpson's *Tempo and Mode* (1944) integrated paleontology with the Modern Synthesis. Gould + Eldredge (1972) introduced punctuated equilibrium; Raup + Sepkoski (1982) established the Big Five mass extinctions quantitatively; Whittington + Conway Morris re-described the Burgess Shale + redefined the Cambrian Explosion. The 21st c added molecular paleobiology (Pääbo's 2022 Nobel for aDNA + Denisovan discovery; Schweitzer + Asara's T. rex collagen; Bailleul's cell preservation; Cappellini's paleoproteomics) + computational tomography + the Paleobiology Database (Alroy). Concludes: paleontology is now a molecular + statistical + computational science synthesizing two centuries of descriptive heritage.
